rows.question: How are redirects followed, and where is the maximum number of redirects enforced?
rows.answer: Redirects are followed by SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects, a generator that loops while a redirect target exists: it copies the prepared request, appends the previous response to history, consumes/releases the connection, normalizes the URL (handling scheme-less "//" URLs and preserving fragments), then calls self.send with allow_redirects=False and extracts the next redirect target via get_redirect_target (src/requests/sessions.py:186-235, src/requests/sessions.py:282-307). The redirect target is obtained from the response's Location header when resp.is_redirect (src/requests/sessions.py:127-152). The maximum number of redirects is enforced inside resolve_redirects: if len(resp.history) >= self.max_redirects it raises TooManyRedirects (src/requests/sessions.py:186-235); the TooManyRedirects exception is defined in src/requests/exceptions.py:102-162. Session.send invokes resolve_redirects when allow_redirects is true (src/requests/sessions.py:801-829).

rows.question: Where is the Authorization header removed when a redirect goes to a different host?
rows.answer: The Authorization header is removed in SessionRedirectMixin.rebuild_auth, which deletes headers["Authorization"] when should_strip_auth returns True for a redirect to a different host (src/requests/sessions.py:309-332). The decision to strip is made in should_strip_auth, which returns True when the old and new hostnames differ (src/requests/sessions.py:154-184).

arguments.query: Authorization header removed redirect different host

rows.question: How does a POST request become a GET after a 303 See Other redirect?
rows.answer: When a redirect response is received, SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects copies the original prepared request and calls self.rebuild_method(prepared_request, resp) to adjust the method (src/requests/sessions.py:237-280). rebuild_method checks the response status code and, per RFC 7231 section 6.4.4, if the status is 303 See Other and the original method is not HEAD, it sets the method to GET (src/requests/sessions.py:370-392). After the method is changed, resolve_redirects also purges the Content-Length, Content-Type, and Transfer-Encoding headers and sets the body to None for redirects other than 307/308, so the new GET request is sent without the original POST body (src/requests/sessions.py:237-280).

arguments.query: 303 See Other redirect POST GET method change

rows.question: How are automatic retries configured for the connection pool?
rows.answer: Automatic retries for the connection pool are configured through the HTTPAdapter's max_retries parameter. In __init__, if max_retries equals DEFAULT_RETRIES, self.max_retries is set to Retry(0, read=False) (no retries); otherwise it is set via Retry.from_int(max_retries) (src/requests/adapters.py:201-237). The class docstring explains that max_retries is the maximum number of retries each connection should attempt, applies only to failed DNS lookups, socket connections and connection timeouts (never to requests where data reached the server), and that by default Requests does not retry failed connections; for granular control you import urllib3's Retry class and pass it instead (src/requests/adapters.py:158-199). The pool itself is created in init_poolmanager, which builds a urllib3 PoolManager with num_pools, maxsize and block, but retries are not passed there—they are handled by the adapter's max_retries (src/requests/adapters.py:239-267).

arguments.query: automatic retries connection pool retry configuration

rows.question: Where are SSL certificates verified and the CA bundle chosen?
rows.answer: SSL certificate verification is performed in HTTPAdapter.cert_verify, which sets conn.cert_reqs to CERT_REQUIRED for https URLs when verify is truthy, and chooses the CA bundle from the user-supplied verify path if given, otherwise from DEFAULT_CA_BUNDLE_PATH, setting conn.ca_certs for a file or conn.ca_cert_dir for a directory (src/requests/adapters.py:307-363). The default CA bundle is provided by the certifi package via where() in src/requests/certs.py:1-18.

rows.question: How is the response body decoded into text when the server sends no charset?
rows.answer: When the server sends no charset, Response.text falls back to self.apparent_encoding, which guesses the encoding using charset_normalizer or chardet, and then decodes the bytes with that encoding (or utf-8 if still None) using errors='replace' (src/requests/models.py:1055-1089). The header-based encoding is obtained from get_encoding_from_headers, which returns None when there is no content-type or no charset parameter, and only defaults to ISO-8859-1 for text/* or utf-8 for application/json (src/requests/utils.py:569-587).

arguments.query: decode response body charset text encoding

rows.question: How does streaming a download in chunks work?
rows.answer: Streaming a download in chunks is done by passing stream=True to the request so the response body is not read into memory all at once (src/requests/sessions.py:601-653), then iterating over the response with Response.iter_content, which yields the data in pieces of chunk_size bytes (src/requests/models.py:914-965). If the underlying raw response has a stream method (the urllib3 case), iter_content delegates to self.raw.stream(chunk_size, decode_content=True), converting ProtocolError, DecodeError, ReadTimeoutError and SSLError into ChunkedEncodingError, ContentDecodingError, ConnectionError and RequestsSSLError respectively; otherwise it repeatedly calls self.raw.read(chunk_size) until an empty chunk is returned (src/requests/models.py:914-965). When the content has already been consumed, it instead slices the stored bytes with iter_slices, which yields successive slices of slice_length (src/requests/models.py:967-977, src/requests/utils.py:569-630). If decode_unicode is True, the chunks are passed through stream_decode_response_unicode, which uses an incremental decoder for the response encoding and yields decoded text, or yields the raw bytes when no encoding is set (src/requests/utils.py:569-630). A chunk_size of None behaves differently: with stream=True it reads data as it arrives in whatever size the chunks are received, while with stream=False the data is returned as a single chunk (src/requests/models.py:914-965). For line-oriented streaming, iter_lines wraps iter_content and splits each chunk on the delimiter or newlines, carrying over a trailing partial line as pending until the next chunk completes it (src/requests/models.py:979-1032).

rows.question: How is JSON parsed from a response, and what error is raised if the body is not valid JSON?
rows.answer: Response.json decodes the body with complexjson.loads (an alias for the json/simplejson module). If no encoding is set and the content is longer than 3 bytes, it first guesses the UTF variant via guess_json_utf and decodes the raw bytes; a UnicodeDecodeError is swallowed and it falls through to decoding self.text. In either path, a JSONDecodeError is caught and re-raised as requests.exceptions.JSONDecodeError (RequestsJSONDecodeError), constructed with the original error's msg, doc and pos (src/requests/models.py:1091-1142). That exception subclasses InvalidJSONError and the compat JSONDecodeError (src/requests/exceptions.py:42-66), with InvalidJSONError itself a RequestException (src/requests/exceptions.py:1-39).

arguments.query: parse JSON from response body invalid JSON error

rows.question: Where is HTTP Digest authentication implemented?
rows.answer: HTTP Digest authentication is implemented in the HTTPDigestAuth class in src/requests/auth.py:124-155, which defines the class and its per-thread state initialization. The digest header is built in build_digest_header (src/requests/auth.py:157-266), the request is prepared and hooks are registered in __call__ (src/requests/auth.py:321-354), and the 401 challenge is handled in handle_401 (src/requests/auth.py:268-319).

rows.question: How is the value of the Basic auth header built?
rows.answer: The Basic auth header value is built by _basic_auth_str, which first coerces non-string username/password to str (with a deprecation warning), then encodes any str username and password to bytes using latin1, joins them with a colon (b":".join((username, password))), base64-encodes the result with b64encode, strips whitespace, converts it to a native string with to_native_string, and prefixes it with "Basic " (src/requests/auth.py:34-82). HTTPBasicAuth.__call__ assigns this value to the Authorization header, and HTTPProxyAuth.__call__ assigns it to Proxy-Authorization (src/requests/auth.py:85-121).

rows.question: How does the library decide whether a URL should bypass the proxy?
rows.answer: The decision is made by should_bypass_proxies(url, no_proxy) in src/requests/utils.py:810-870. It first resolves no_proxy from the argument or the NO_PROXY/no_proxy environment variable (lowercase preferred over uppercase). It parses the URL and returns True immediately if the URL has no hostname (e.g. file:// URLs). If no_proxy is set, it splits it on commas (ignoring spaces) and matches the hostname: for IPv4 addresses it checks CIDR membership via address_in_network or exact IP equality; for other hosts it compares the hostname and the hostname:port string against each entry, both exactly and as a suffix after prepending a dot (so '.example.com' matches 'sub.example.com'). If no no_proxy match is found, it calls the platform proxy_bypass(hostname) (with the original no_proxy environment value restored via set_environ), catching TypeError and socket.gaierror as False; if that returns True the URL bypasses the proxy, otherwise it does not. On Windows, proxy_bypass checks the environment (proxy_bypass_environment) or the registry ProxyOverride list, treating '<local>' as hosts without a dot and converting '*' and '?' into regex wildcards (src/requests/utils.py:96-146). get_environ_proxies uses this result: if should_bypass_proxies is True it returns an empty dict, otherwise it returns getproxies() (src/requests/utils.py:873-908).

arguments.query: bypass proxy URL should bypass proxy

rows.question: Where are proxy settings read from environment variables?
rows.answer: Proxy settings are read from environment variables in get_environ_proxies, which calls getproxies() (src/requests/utils.py:873-908). This is used by Session.merge_environment_settings to set the environment's proxies when trust_env is true (src/requests/sessions.py:831-886), and by resolve_proxies, which calls get_environ_proxies when trust_env is set and the URL is not bypassed (src/requests/utils.py:911-962). On Windows, proxy_bypass checks getproxies_environment() before falling back to the registry (src/requests/utils.py:96-146).

rows.question: How are query parameters URL-encoded into the request URL?
rows.answer: Query parameters are URL-encoded by PreparedRequest.prepare_url, which calls _encode_params on the params (src/requests/models.py:544-563). _encode_params converts the data into a list of (key, value) byte pairs via to_key_val_list, encoding each key and value as UTF-8, then returns urlencode(result, doseq=True) (src/requests/models.py:108-180). The resulting encoded string is appended to the existing query with an '&' separator if a query already exists, otherwise it becomes the query, and the full URL is rebuilt with urlunparse and passed through requote_uri (src/requests/models.py:544-563).

arguments.query: URL encode query parameters request URL

rows.question: How are multipart file uploads encoded?
rows.answer: Multipart file uploads are encoded as multipart/form-data. When files are provided, prepare_body calls _encode_files, which builds the body and returns the content type (src/requests/models.py:603-630). _encode_files converts each file into a RequestField, calls make_multipart on it, and then calls encode_multipart_formdata to produce the final body and content type (src/requests/models.py:182-251). The multipart content type constant is defined as "multipart/form-data" (src/requests/auth.py:1-31).

rows.question: How is the Content-Length of a request body computed?
rows.answer: The Content-Length is computed by PreparedRequest.prepare_content_length, which calls super_len(body) and, if a length is returned, sets the Content-Length header to that value; if the body is None and the method is not GET or HEAD, it sets Content-Length to 0 (src/requests/models.py:654-697). super_len determines the length by first encoding a str to utf-8 (for urllib3 2.x+), then using len(o) if the object has __len__, else o.len if it has a len attribute, else os.fstat(o.fileno()).st_size for file-like objects, warning if the file is not opened in binary mode (src/requests/utils.py:160-199). For streamed/iterable bodies, prepare_body calls super_len(data) and sets Content-Length if a length is found, otherwise sets Transfer-Encoding: chunked (src/requests/models.py:603-652).

rows.question: How are cookies from a response stored in the cookie jar?
rows.answer: Cookies from a response are stored by extract_cookies_to_jar, which wraps the response's original HTTPMessage headers in a MockResponse and the PreparedRequest in a MockRequest, then calls jar.extract_cookies(res, req) so http.cookiejar parses and stores the Set-Cookie headers into the jar (src/requests/cookies.py:114-161).

arguments.query: store cookies from response in cookie jar

rows.question: How are session-level settings merged with per-request settings?
rows.answer: Session-level and per-request settings are merged by the merge_setting function, which prefers the explicit per-request value: if the session setting is None it returns the request setting, if the request setting is None it returns the session setting, and if both are mappings it builds a new dict from the session setting then updates it with the request setting, finally dropping any keys whose value is None (src/requests/sessions.py:76-124). This is applied in Session.prepare_request for headers, params, and auth, while hooks use merge_hooks, which falls back to the request hooks when the session hooks are None or have an empty 'response' list, and to the session hooks when the request hooks are None or have an empty 'response' list, otherwise delegating to merge_setting (src/requests/sessions.py:505-555, src/requests/sessions.py:76-124). For proxies, stream, verify, and cert, Session.merge_environment_settings first gathers environment values when trust_env is set, then merges each with the corresponding session attribute via merge_setting (src/requests/sessions.py:831-886).

arguments.query: session-level settings merged with per-request settings

rows.question: How does a session pick which transport adapter handles a URL?
rows.answer: A session picks the transport adapter by iterating over its mounted adapters in order and returning the first one whose prefix matches the start of the URL, comparing case-insensitively; if none match it raises InvalidSchema (src/requests/sessions.py:831-886). Adapters are registered via mount, which stores the adapter under its prefix and reorders the adapters dict so longer prefixes come first, ensuring the most specific prefix wins (src/requests/sessions.py:888-905).

rows.question: Where are default headers such as User-Agent set?
rows.answer: Default headers such as User-Agent are built by default_headers() in src/requests/utils.py:911-962, which returns a CaseInsensitiveDict containing User-Agent (from default_user_agent()), Accept-Encoding, Accept, and Connection. These are assigned to a Session's headers in Session.__init__ at src/requests/sessions.py:442-488 via self.headers = default_headers().

rows.question: How are HTTP header names handled case-insensitively?
rows.answer: HTTP header names are handled case-insensitively by the CaseInsensitiveDict class, which stores each header under its lowercased key while remembering the original case of the last key set (src/requests/structures.py:20-74). When a header is set, __setitem__ uses key.lower() as the lookup key but stores the actual key alongside the value (src/requests/structures.py:66-69). Lookups via __getitem__ and deletions via __delitem__ also use key.lower(), so querying is case-insensitive (src/requests/structures.py:70-74). Iteration returns the original cased keys (src/requests/structures.py:71-72), and lower_items yields all-lowercase keys (src/requests/structures.py:76-78). Equality comparison is case-insensitive by comparing lower_items (src/requests/structures.py:79-85). PreparedRequest.prepare_headers creates a CaseInsensitiveDict and stores each header name converted to a native string (src/requests/models.py:565-574).

rows.question: How are event hooks such as the response hook dispatched?
rows.answer: Event hooks are dispatched by dispatch_hook, which looks up the hook list for the given event key in the hooks dictionary, normalizes a single callable into a list, then calls each hook in order with the hook data (the Response) and any extra kwargs, replacing the data with the hook's return value when it is not None, and finally returns the resulting data (src/requests/hooks.py:31-48). The only supported event is 'response' (src/requests/hooks.py:22-22). Hooks are registered on a request via RequestHooksMixin.register_hook, which appends a callable or extends with an iterable of callables, raising ValueError for unsupported events (src/requests/models.py:254-281). During a request, Session.send obtains the request's hooks and, after the adapter produces the response, calls dispatch_hook('response', hooks, r, **kwargs) to run the response hooks (src/requests/sessions.py:752-799).

rows.question: Where is the Link header parsed into a dictionary?
rows.answer: The Link header is parsed into a dictionary by the `links` property on `Response`, which reads the `link` header, calls `parse_header_links`, and builds a dict keyed by `rel` or `url` (src/requests/models.py:1091-1142). The underlying parsing into per-link dicts is done by `parse_header_links` (src/requests/utils.py:965-1005).

rows.question: How does raising for HTTP error status codes build its error message?
rows.answer: Response.raise_for_status builds the message by first normalizing self.reason: if it is bytes it tries to decode as utf-8 and falls back to iso-8859-1 on UnicodeDecodeError, otherwise it uses the reason as-is (src/requests/models.py:1144-1184). It then sets http_error_msg to an f-string of the form "{status_code} Client Error: {reason} for url: {url}" when 400 <= status_code < 500, or "{status_code} Server Error: {reason} for url: {url}" when 500 <= status_code < 600 (src/requests/models.py:1144-1184). If the message is non-empty it raises HTTPError with that message and the response attached (src/requests/models.py:1144-1184).

arguments.query: raise HTTP error status code error message

rows.question: How are connect and read timeouts passed down to urllib3?
rows.answer: In HTTPAdapter.send, the timeout argument is normalized into a urllib3 Timeout object (imported as TimeoutSauce from urllib3.util): if it is a tuple, the two values are unpacked as connect and read and passed to TimeoutSauce(connect=connect, read=read); if it is already a TimeoutSauce it is used as-is; otherwise a single value is used for both connect and read (src/requests/adapters.py:681-693). The resulting resolved_timeout is then passed to conn.urlopen as timeout=resolved_timeout (src/requests/adapters.py:695-748).

rows.question: Where are credentials loaded from the user's netrc file?
rows.answer: Credentials are loaded from the user's netrc file by get_netrc_auth, which checks the NETRC environment variable first and otherwise looks for ~/.netrc or ~/.netrc (NETRC_FILES) in the user's home directory (src/requests/utils.py:231-287). The file location is defined by NETRC_FILES = (".netrc", "_netrc") (src/requests/utils.py:74-74).

rows.question: What does `prepare_url` do with internationalized (IDNA) host names?
rows.answer: prepare_url IDNA-encodes the host when it contains non-ASCII characters: it checks unicode_is_ascii(host), and if false it calls self._get_idna_encoded_host(host), which runs idna.encode(host, uts46=True).decode("utf-8") and raises UnicodeError (surfaced as InvalidURL "URL has an invalid label.") on idna.IDNAError; for ASCII hosts it only rejects labels starting with "*" or "." (src/requests/models.py:483-542, src/requests/models.py:424-481).

rows.question: What does `requote_uri` do?
rows.answer: requote_uri re-quotes a URI by passing it through an unquote/quote cycle so it is fully and consistently quoted: it first unquotes only unreserved characters via unquote_unreserved and then quotes only illegal characters, keeping reserved, unreserved and '%' characters safe (safe_with_percent = "!#$%&'()*+,/:;=?@[]~"); if the URI cannot be unquoted (InvalidURL), it quotes the original URI with safe_without_percent = "!#$&'()*+,/:;=?@[]~" so any unquoted '%' characters are properly escaped (src/requests/utils.py:704-722).

rows.question: How does `rewind_body` work?
rows.answer: rewind_body moves a file-like request body's pointer back to its recorded starting position so it can be read again on redirect (src/requests/utils.py:1098-1155). It gets the body's seek method via getattr(prepared_request.body, "seek", None); if that exists and prepared_request._body_position is an integer, it calls body_seek(prepared_request._body_position), raising UnrewindableBodyError if an OSError occurs; otherwise it raises UnrewindableBodyError because the body cannot be rewound (src/requests/utils.py:1098-1155). The _body_position value is recorded in prepare_body by calling body.tell() before reading, or set to object() if tell() fails (src/requests/models.py:603-652). It is called from resolve_redirects when the request is rewindable, i.e. _body_position is not None and the headers contain Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding (src/requests/sessions.py:237-280, src/requests/sessions.py:282-307).

rows.question: What does `get_connection_with_tls_context` do?
rows.answer: get_connection_with_tls_context returns a urllib3 HTTPConnectionPool for a given PreparedRequest and TLS settings; it is intended only for subclassing HTTPAdapter, not direct user code (src/requests/adapters.py:455-510). It asserts the request is prepared, selects a proxy via select_proxy, builds host and pool-key attributes through build_connection_pool_key_attributes (raising InvalidURL on ValueError), and then obtains the connection either from a proxy manager (validating the proxy URL and raising InvalidProxyURL if the host is missing) or from the default poolmanager (src/requests/adapters.py:455-510). The TLS-related pool key attributes are produced by _urllib3_request_context, which sets cert_reqs to CERT_NONE when verify is False, sets ca_certs or ca_cert_dir when verify is a string, and sets cert_file/key_file when a client certificate is provided (src/requests/adapters.py:70-119).

rows.question: Explain `CaseInsensitiveDict.lower_items`.
rows.answer: CaseInsensitiveDict.lower_items returns a generator of (lowercased_key, value) tuples, like items() but with all keys lowercased (src/requests/structures.py:76-78). It iterates over self._store.items(), where each entry is a (lowerkey, (original_key, value)) pair, and yields (lowerkey, value) (src/requests/structures.py:76-78). It is used by __eq__ to compare two mappings case-insensitively by building dicts from lower_items on both sides (src/requests/structures.py:76-93).

rows.question: My Authorization header disappears after the server redirects me. Why?
rows.answer: requests deliberately strips the Authorization header on redirects to avoid leaking credentials. When a redirect happens, rebuild_auth checks whether the header should be removed via should_strip_auth and, if so, deletes it from the prepared request (src/requests/sessions.py:309-332). should_strip_auth returns True whenever the hostname changes, and also when the port or scheme changes on the same host, except for the special case of an http (port 80/None) to https (port 443/None) redirect on the same host, which is kept for backwards compatibility (src/requests/sessions.py:154-184). So if your redirect goes to a different host, or changes scheme/port (other than the http->https same-host case), the Authorization header is removed.

rows.question: response.text shows garbled characters for a page that has no charset in its headers
rows.answer: When the response headers carry no charset, Response.text falls back to self.apparent_encoding, which guesses the encoding using charset_normalizer or chardet; if that still yields nothing it decodes with utf-8 and errors='replace', so wrong guesses show up as garbled characters (src/requests/models.py:1034-1089). The header-based encoding comes from get_encoding_from_headers, which returns None when there is no content-type, ISO-8859-1 for text/*, and utf-8 for application/json (src/requests/utils.py:569-630). To fix garbled output, set r.encoding to the correct value before accessing r.text (src/requests/models.py:1034-1089).

rows.question: Uploading a file object that was partially read sends the wrong Content-Length
rows.answer: For a file-like object that has been partially read, super_len computes the Content-Length as the remaining bytes, not the full file size: it reads current_position = o.tell(), and if the object has seek but no usable fileno it seeks to the end to get total_length, then seeks back to current_position, finally returning max(0, total_length - current_position) (src/requests/utils.py:201-228). This value is then set as the Content-Length header in prepare_body for streamed bodies (src/requests/models.py:603-652) and in prepare_content_length for non-streamed bodies (src/requests/models.py:654-697).

arguments.query: upload file object partially read Content-Length
partially read file-like object seek current_position total_length super_len

rows.question: I get a TooManyRedirects exception. Where is it raised?
rows.answer: TooManyRedirects is raised in SessionRedirectMixin.resolve_redirects when the number of redirects reaches self.max_redirects (src/requests/sessions.py:186-235). The exception class itself is defined in src/requests/exceptions.py:102-162.

rows.question: Requests ignores my NO_PROXY environment variable
rows.answer: Requests does honor NO_PROXY, but only when the session trusts the environment (trust_env is True, the default). The check is done in should_bypass_proxies, which reads the no_proxy environment variable (lowercase preferred over uppercase) and returns True if the URL's hostname matches an entry in the comma-separated no_proxy list (exact host, host:port, or a suffix match), or if the platform's proxy_bypass reports a bypass (src/requests/utils.py:810-870). get_environ_proxies returns an empty dict when should_bypass_proxies is True, so no proxy is applied (src/requests/utils.py:873-882). resolve_proxies only consults environment proxies when trust_env is True and the URL is not bypassed, and it also honors a 'no_proxy' key passed in the proxies dict (src/requests/utils.py:911-937). If you set trust_env=False, or pass an explicit proxies dict that overrides the scheme, the NO_PROXY environment variable will not be applied, which is the usual reason it appears to be ignored (src/requests/sessions.py:334-368).

rows.question: A header value containing a newline raises InvalidHeader
How does closing a session release its transport adapters?
rows.answer: Session.close() iterates over the values of self.adapters and calls close() on each one, which disposes of the adapter's internal state (src/requests/sessions.py:883-886). For the default HTTPAdapter, close() clears the pool manager and every active proxy manager, which closes any pooled connections (src/requests/adapters.py:555-563). The base BaseAdapter.close() is the hook that subclasses override to clean up adapter-specific items (src/requests/adapters.py:152-155).

rows.question: How are outgoing request headers validated and stored case-insensitively?
rows.answer: Outgoing request headers are validated and stored case-insensitively in PreparedRequest.prepare_headers, which creates a CaseInsensitiveDict, iterates over the provided header items, calls check_header_validity on each header to raise an exception on invalid values, and stores each header using to_native_string(name) as the key (src/requests/models.py:565-574). The case-insensitive storage is provided by CaseInsensitiveDict, which remembers the case of the last key set but performs querying and contains testing case-insensitively (src/requests/structures.py:20-74). Header part validation is done by _validate_header_part, which selects a str or bytes validator based on the part's type and raises InvalidHeader if the part does not match, reporting whether the invalid part was the header name or value (src/requests/utils.py:1098-1155).

arguments.query: outgoing request headers validated stored case-insensitively

rows.question: How does closing a response release its underlying connection?
rows.answer: Response.close() releases the connection by first closing the underlying raw stream if the content has not been consumed, then calling the raw object's release_conn method to return the connection to the pool (src/requests/models.py:1144-1184).

rows.question: How is a dictionary converted to a cookie jar while respecting overwrite?
rows.answer: cookiejar_from_dict builds a RequestsCookieJar (or uses the provided jar), collects the names of cookies already in the jar, then for each key in the dictionary it calls set_cookie with create_cookie only when overwrite is True or the name is not already present in the jar (src/requests/cookies.py:579-601).

arguments.query: dictionary converted to cookie jar overwrite

rows.question: Which Python versions does requests officially support?
rows.answer: Requests officially supports Python 3.10+ (README.md:30-38).

rows.question: How do I install requests?
rows.answer: Run `python -m pip install requests` in your terminal (docs/user/install.rst:10-15). Alternatively, clone the source from GitHub and install it with `python -m pip install .` (docs/user/install.rst:17-36).

rows.question: What are the runtime dependencies of requests?
rows.answer: The runtime dependencies of requests are charset_normalizer>=2,<4, idna>=2.5,<4, urllib3>=1.26,<3, and certifi>=2023.5.7 (pyproject.toml:1-24).

rows.question: How do I run the test suite?
rows.answer: Run the test suite with `make test`, which executes `python -m pytest tests` (Makefile:1-27). For CI-style runs with a JUnit report, use `make ci`, which runs `python -m pytest tests --junitxml=report.xml` (Makefile:1-27). You can also run coverage with `make coverage` (Makefile:1-27).

rows.question: How do I set a timeout on a request?
rows.answer: Pass the timeout parameter to the request call. A single value applies to both the connect and read timeouts, e.g. requests.get('https://github.com', timeout=5) (docs/user/advanced.rst:1086-1117). To set them separately, pass a tuple (connect, read), e.g. requests.get('https://github.com', timeout=(3.05, 27)) (docs/user/advanced.rst:1086-1117). You can also pass timeout=None to wait forever (docs/user/advanced.rst:1119-1137). The timeout is not a limit on the entire response download; an exception is raised if no bytes are received on the socket for timeout seconds (docs/user/quickstart.rst:529-549).

arguments.query: set a timeout on a request

rows.question: How do I use HTTP basic authentication?
rows.answer: Use the auth argument with either an HTTPBasicAuth object or a (username, password) tuple. Example: from requests.auth import HTTPBasicAuth; basic = HTTPBasicAuth('user', 'pass'); requests.get('https://httpbin.org/basic-auth/user/pass', auth=basic) (docs/user/authentication.rst:13-33). The shorthand requests.get('https://httpbin.org/basic-auth/user/pass', auth=('user', 'pass')) is exactly the same as the HTTPBasicAuth example (docs/user/authentication.rst:13-33). If no auth is given, Requests may read credentials from the user's netrc file at ~/.netrc, ~/_netrc, or the NETRC environment variable, and disable this by setting trust_env to False on a Session (docs/user/authentication.rst:36-56).

rows.question: How do I configure proxies?
rows.answer: You can configure proxies in three ways. Per request, pass a proxies dict to any request method, e.g. requests.get('http://example.org', proxies={'http': 'http://10.10.1.10:3128', 'https': 'http://10.10.1.10:1080'}) (docs/user/advanced.rst:578-614). For a whole session, do session = requests.Session(); session.proxies.update(proxies) then session.get(...) (docs/user/advanced.rst:578-614); note that session.proxies values may be overwritten by environmental proxies, so explicitly passing proxies on each request is safer (docs/user/advanced.rst:578-614). Or set standard environment variables http_proxy, https_proxy, no_proxy, all_proxy (uppercase variants also supported), e.g. export HTTP_PROXY="http://10.10.1.10:3128" (docs/user/advanced.rst:614-645). For HTTP Basic Auth use the http://user:password@host/ syntax in the proxy URL (docs/user/advanced.rst:614-645). For a specific scheme and host, use the scheme://hostname form as the key, e.g. proxies = {'http://10.20.1.128': 'http://10.10.1.10:5323'} (docs/user/advanced.rst:647-691). Proxy URLs must include the scheme (docs/user/advanced.rst:647-691). For HTTPS through a proxy, trust the proxy's root certificate by setting REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE (or CURL_CA_BUNDLE) to a certificate file (docs/user/advanced.rst:647-691). SOCKS proxies are supported via pip install 'requests[socks]' with schemes socks5 (client-side DNS) or socks5h (proxy-side DNS) (docs/user/advanced.rst:647-695).

rows.question: How do I verify SSL certificates or turn verification off?
rows.answer: Requests verifies SSL certificates for HTTPS requests by default, and throws an SSLError if it cannot verify the certificate (docs/user/advanced.rst:211-244). To verify against a specific CA, pass verify the path to a CA_BUNDLE file or a directory of trusted CA certificates, e.g. requests.get('https://github.com', verify='/path/to/certfile'), or set it persistently on a session with s.verify = '/path/to/certfile' (docs/user/advanced.rst:211-244). If verify points to a directory, it must have been processed with the c_rehash utility from OpenSSL (docs/user/advanced.rst:211-244). You can also set the trusted CAs via the REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE environment variable, with CURL_CA_BUNDLE as a fallback (docs/user/advanced.rst:211-244). To turn verification off, set verify to False, e.g. requests.get('https://kennethreitz.org', verify=False); note this accepts any TLS certificate and ignores hostname mismatches and expired certificates, making the application vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks, so it is only recommended for local development or testing (docs/user/advanced.rst:243-252).

arguments.query: verify SSL certificates turn verification off

rows.question: What is a Session object and why would I use one?
rows.answer: A Session object is a Requests session that provides cookie persistence, connection-pooling, and configuration (src/requests/sessions.py:395-440). You would use one to keep cookies, headers, auth, proxies, and other settings consistent across multiple requests, and it can be used as a context manager (src/requests/sessions.py:395-440).

rows.question: How do I contribute a change to requests?
rows.answer: To contribute a change to requests, first read the Contributor's Guide and the AI Policy before opening any issues or proposing pull requests (.github/CONTRIBUTING.md:1-8). The Contributor's Guide lays out guidelines and advice for contributing, and is split into sections based on the type of contribution you're thinking of making (docs/dev/contributing.rst:1-23). Note that maintainers have the last word on whether a contribution is suitable, and contributions may be rejected if they do not suit the project's current goals (docs/dev/contributing.rst:49-59). When submitting a pull request, you certify that you are the author or have the legal right to submit it, hold the copyright or have authorization, understand the code, and accept full responsibility for it (.github/AI_POLICY.md:1-27).
